critical_point: find() returns -1 for a missing text, which can be mistaken for a real position, while index() raises a ValueError.
stem: A program tests 'if line.find("error"):' to see whether a log line holds the word error. Which reason shows that this test is unreliable?
options_or_blanks: find hands back a position: 0 when the word starts the line (false) and -1 when it is missing (true)
find works only on lines that are shorter than ten characters
find changes the line to lower case before it looks for the word
find hands back the word itself, which is never false
reason: find gives the index of the first match or -1; a match at position 0 is false in an if, while the -1 of a missing word is true.
question: Q3
tip: find tells where a text starts inside another text, counting from zero.

critical_point: A function must be defined before the line that calls it runs.
stem: A script calls show() on its last line. What changes if the def of show is moved below that call, to the end of the file?
options_or_blanks: Nothing changes, because Python reads the whole file before it runs the first line
The call stops with a NameError, because the def has not run yet when the call is reached
The function runs twice, once at the call and once at the def
The call prints None, because the function is still empty
reason: def only stores the function when its line runs; a call placed before the def meets a name that does not exist yet.
question: Q4
tip: A NameError means Python met an unknown name; a def line stores its name only when reached.

critical_point: Deleting by index from the front forward goes wrong because the later items move down one place.
stem: Read the program, then choose what it prints and what the opposite order of the two del lines would print.
options_or_blanks: [6, 8], and [7, 8] in the opposite order: after a deletion the later items move down one place
[6, 8], and [6, 8] in the opposite order: the order of deletions never matters
[7, 8], and [6, 8] in the opposite order: del counts from the back
[6, 7], and [7, 8] in the opposite order: del removes the item at the end
reason: After del items[0] the list is [6, 7, 8], so index 1 is now 7 and [6, 8] remains; the opposite order removes 6 and then 5, leaving [7, 8].
question: Q5
tip: After a deletion the items behind it move down one place, so the indexes shift.

critical_point: Removing or adding pairs while looping over a dictionary raises an error.
stem: Read the program, then choose what happens when it runs and the reason for it.
options_or_blanks: It prints {'ink': 3}: the pair with a zero is deleted and the loop goes on
It prints {'pen': 0, 'ink': 3}: del does nothing inside a loop
It stops with an error: a dictionary may not change its size while a loop reads it
It prints {}: del removes every pair when one pair is deleted
reason: Deleting a pair while looping over the dictionary raises a RuntimeError; build a new dictionary or loop over a list of the keys instead.
question: Q5
tip: A dictionary stores pairs of key and value, and a loop over it reads those pairs one after another.
